newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan prepares public opinion for war.
newsitem.headline: Sudan prepares public opinion for war.

text.p: The Sudanese government on Monday prepared public opinion for a military campaign after the army said Ethiopian forces had attacked two border towns.
State radio and television broadcast patriotic and military songs and poetry, along with messages supporting the government and attacking what they called the Ethiopian aggression.

The radio said the Osman Digna brigade of the paramilitary People's Defence Forces was preparing to leave Khartoum towards the border towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan, about 600 km (360 miles) southeast of the capital.

Sudanese rebels say they captured Kurmuk and some army garrisons in Blue Nile province on Sunday in the first big combined operation by northern and southern opponents of the Islamist-dominated government in Khartoum.
An armed forces statement referred only obliquely to a rebel role, saying that Ethiopian forces were operating along with what it called "remnants of agents and mercenaries".
The radio said members of the public had started to go to enlist at offices of the People's Defence Forces, a force set up after the 1989 coup to help the army fight southern rebels.

First Vice President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh told one group of recruits on Monday that Sudan was ready to defend itself and would not abandon its Islamic orientation -- the government's term for the gradual Islamisation of Sudanese society.
The National Congress, the country's only political organisation, called for a mass demonstration on Tuesday morning to protest against the attack on the border.
Ministers of state in the foreign ministry briefed foreign ambassadors on Sudan's view of the attack.
President Omar Hassan al-Bashir has called for "general mobilisation" against the threat but the government has not announced any specific compulsory measures.
In the streets of Khartoum, life continued as normal, with people going about their daily business.
In Cairo a spokesman for the opposition National Democratic Alliance said the attacks in Blue Nile province had been a big blow to the government. "It is in a panic," he added.
But the spokesman, Farouq Abu Eissa, told Reuters the opposition forces did not envisage advancing on Khartoum.
"The operations are to distract and weaken the...government so the uprising can take place," he said.

Opposition leader Sadeq al-Mahdi, the democratically elected prime minister overthrown by Bashir in 1989, also said this month in Cairo he believed that change would come through an uprising, rather than from military action from abroad.
